http:
  addr: "127.0.0.1:18113"
  read_timeout: 5s
  write_timeout: 0s  # 0s = none: streamed answers run longer than a fixed write deadline
  idle_timeout: 120s
  startup_timeout: 30s
  shutdown_timeout: 10s
  readiness_timeout: 15s

# Diagnostic pprof endpoints are opt-in and loopback-only. Use an SSH tunnel
# or an equivalent protected local access path when profiling a remote host.
profiling:
  enabled: false
  addr: "127.0.0.1:6063"

middleware:
  timeout: 30s
  logger:
    level: error  # dev | prod

documents:
  mode: "upload-only"       # upload-only | mirror; mirror removes missing files under documents.paths
  paths:
    - "samples"
  ignore_patterns: []

ingest:
  max_attempts: 3
  initial_interval: 500ms
  max_interval: 10s
  multiplier: 2.0
  workers: 8
  max_file_bytes: 16777216       # 16 MiB per document upload/source file
  max_upload_bytes: 67108864    # 64 MiB per multipart request
  embed_batch_size: 64           # bound each Ollama embedding request
  max_chunks_per_file: 10000     # reject pathological documents before indexing

qdrant:
  addr: "127.0.0.1:17444"
  collection: "p1_documents_20261003"
  top_k: 5
  prefetch_mul: 5  # store-level candidate multiplier for hybrid search legs

embedder:
  provider: "ollama"
  model: "embeddinggemma-300m-q8:latest"
  ollama_addr: "http://localhost:11434"
  dimensions: 768
  request_timeout: 60s
  query_prefix: "task: search result | query: "   # prepended to queries at search time (EmbeddingGemma task instruction; empty = off)
  # num_gpu: 0               # optional: keep embeddings on CPU when a larger answer model occupies the GPU; omitted = Ollama placement
  document_prefix: "title: none | text: "          # prepended to chunks at ingest time; requires reindex when changed
  max_input_chars: 8000                            # rune-clamp on dense embed inputs so Ollama never truncates silently (0 = off)

chunker:
  provider: "recursive"  # recursive | sentence-window (measured 2026-09-27, ADR 0033: recursive stays)
  chunk_size: 512
  chunk_overlap: 64
  window_size: 3          # sentences before+after each sentence (sentence-window only)

search:
  max_query_chars: 8192
  max_fragments: 16
  max_concurrent_fragments: 8
  max_top_k: 50
  max_chunks_per_file: 3
  fusion:
    enabled: false # enable only after offline golden-set evidence supports the candidate policy
    rrf_k: 60
    dense_weight: 1.0
    bm25_weight: 1.0
    exact_match_boost: 0.0
    header_match_boost: 0.0
    min_exact_tokens: 1
    min_header_tokens: 1
    profiles: {}

reranker:
  enabled: false   # opt in only after a measured gain on the current embedding profile
  addr: "http://localhost:5002"
  model: "BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3" # swappable sidecar cross-encoder (env RERANKER_MODEL overrides); revert to cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 for the tiny/fast baseline
  candidate_mul: 4     # fetch topK*4 candidates before reranking (more headroom for the reranker to reorder)
  request_timeout: 30s
  adaptive_enabled: false # opt in until release-gated judgments confirm no quality regression
  adaptive_margin_threshold: 0.01 # rerank when dense/lexical top results disagree or fused top margin is below 1%

# Local inference profile. LLM and embedding concurrency is owned by the
# Ollama scheduler (OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL) plus each role's request_timeout, so
# no client-side gate is imposed. The reranker keeps an explicit client-side
# queue; it is CPU by default for portable laptop operation — use the GPU
# Compose override with device=cuda only when Ollama and the reranker have a
# measured hardware budget.
inference:
  profile: "local"
  ollama:
    keep_alive: 5m
  reranker:
    max_concurrent: 1
    queue_timeout: 30s
    device: "cpu"
    backend: "torch"

# Process-local operation gates (bounded, finite queues). Indexing is
# single-writer; destructive mutations (document reset, chat edits and
# deletions) never run concurrently with an indexing pass. A request that
# waits longer than queue_timeout fails fast instead of piling up. LLM and
# embedding concurrency is NOT gated here — the Ollama scheduler owns it.
# These limits coordinate one API process only; they are not distributed.
gates:
  indexing:
    max_concurrent: 1
    queue_timeout: 5s
  destructive:
    max_concurrent: 1
    queue_timeout: 10s

enrichment:
  # Index-time LLM enrichment (uses Ollama; one-time cost per chunk, zero
  # query-time latency). Changing these requires a reindex to take effect.
  request_timeout: 120s
  contextual:
    enabled: false          # Anthropic-style LLM-written situational context prepended to each chunk before embedding
    ollama_addr: "http://localhost:11434"
    model: "gemma3:1b"

semantic_cache:
  enabled: true     # set true to enable; requires no extra infra (reuses Qdrant)
  collection: "p1_cache_20261003"
  threshold: 0.90    # cosine similarity cutoff (0.85=permissive, 0.95=strict)
  ttl: 24h           # 0 = no expiry

generator:
  enabled: true      # set true + ensure the Ollama model is pulled; the dashboard or POST /api/v1/turns with generate=true
  ollama_addr: "http://localhost:11434"
  model: "gemma3:4b"  # LLM for answer generation; use instruct models. gemma3:4b passes the generation gate (ADR 0034: faithfulness 0.881 / relevancy 0.803 vs 1b 0.750/0.756) at ~9x answer latency; gemma3:1b is the low-latency fallback
  request_timeout: 120s
  max_output_tokens: 512 # bound answer generation; prevents an unending stream
  num_ctx: 4096          # pin the Ollama context window: prompt budget + instructions + output must fit (GENERATOR_NUM_CTX)

chat:
  # Chat use-case tuning: prompt assembly and the streaming turn lifecycle.
  max_context_tokens: 2800  # token budget for retrieved chunks (~70% of 4k ctx window)
  event_buffer: 4096
  max_event_log_bytes: 1048576   # 1 MiB replay log per turn
  max_retained_turns: 64
  finished_turn_ttl: 10m
  persist_timeout: 5s

rewriter:
  # Conversational query rewriting (Rewrite-Retrieve-Read): follow-up turns
  # are rewritten into standalone search queries against the session's last
  # `turns` turns before retrieval, so "what about the second one?" stops
  # searching garbage. Skipped when a session has no prior turns; any
  # rewrite failure falls back to the raw query. Costs +1 LLM call per
  # follow-up turn.
  enabled: true
  turns: 4           # prior turns fed to the rewriter
  request_timeout: 8s
  ollama_addr: "http://localhost:11434"
  model: "gemma3:1b"

history:
  enabled: true              # persists chat sessions/turns to Qdrant, no extra infra
  collection: "p1_history_20261003"
  session_page_size: 50      # sidebar sessions returned per request
  turn_page_size: 500        # Qdrant scroll page used while loading one session

docling:
  enabled: false             # enable PDF intake when the Docling sidecar is available
  addr: "http://localhost:5003"
  request_timeout: 120s

cases.query: A worker finished after its Redis lock expired. Is it safe for it to delete the lock key now?

turn.query: A worker finished after its Redis lock expired. Is it safe for it to delete the lock key now?

results.text: When the worker finishes, it should delete the marker only if the token still matches. Otherwise, a worker whose lock has expired could accidentally delete a newer worker's lock. The lock can also expire while work is still running, allowing another worker to start the same job. For important changes, make the operation safe to repeat or enforce uniqueness in the database that stores the result. A lock alone cannot prevent duplicate work after it expires

A Redis lock is a temporary marker that lets one worker claim a job. SET lock:resource <token> NX PX <milliseconds> creates the marker only if it does not exist (NX) and sets an expiry time (PX). Give each attempt a different token so Redis can tell which worker owns the marker.

Case C: Lock Deletion Safety (Lua Script) If Thread A's lock expires and Thread B acquires the key, Thread A's raw DEL could remove Thread B's lock. DISCO checks the trip ID in an atomic Lua script:
if redis.call("get", KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
    return redis.call("del", KEYS[1])
else
    return 0
end
ult. A lock alone cannot prevent duplicate work after it expires. The Redis distributed-lock guide explains the safety assumptions and failure cases.

Case B: Driver Declines or Times Out
If declined: DISCO deletes the lock with DEL driver:lock:drv_98765.
If timed out: Redis expires the key after 15 seconds. A background timer then tries Candidate #2.

cases.query: I want to avoid losing work when a RabbitMQ consumer crashes. Should I use automatic or manual acknowledgements?

turn.query: I want to avoid losing work when a RabbitMQ consumer crashes. Should I use automatic or manual acknowledgements?

results.text:
Manual acknowledgement (autoAck: false) The application must explicitly call channel.ack(deliveryTag) after successful processing.
nack (or reject) can be used with requeue=true to return the message to the queue, or requeue=false to dead-letter it (if DLX is configured).
Gives full control over at-least-once delivery semantics.

Auto acknowledgement (autoAck: true) The broker considers a message delivered as soon as it sends it over the socket.
Fastest, no risk of forgetting to ack.
Messages can be lost if the consumer crashes before processing.

cases.query: If I create two threads in one process, which memory do they share and which part stays private?

turn.query: If I create two threads in one process, which memory do they share and which part stays private?

results.text:
The memory of one process is shared by all of its threads, but each thread has its own private stack:
Process A: one shared address space
+--------------------------------------+
| Shared by Thread A and Thread B      |
|                                      |
| Code                                 |
| Global / static variables            |
| Heap                                 |
+--------------------------------------+
| Thread A: private stack              |
+--------------------------------------+

Each thread uses its stack for local variables, function calls, and return addresses. Threads in the same process share the code, heap, and global or static data. Shared heap and global data may require synchronization when multiple threads access it concurrently.
Note: A thread can access another thread’s stack memory if it has a valid pointer to that memory.

thread’s stack memory if it has a valid pointer to that memory.
Separate processes have separate address spaces, so their heaps, global data, and stacks are isolated from one another unless they explicitly use an inter-process sharing mechanism.

cases.query: A producer is sending work faster than consumers can handle. What is backpressure supposed to do?

turn.query: A producer is sending work faster than consumers can handle. What is backpressure supposed to do?

results.text:
rebuilds state or falls back to durable storage.
Source of truth

Push and pull event
at-least-once vs exactly-once delivery
Backpressure: limit queues and concurrent work when producers are faster than consumers. Decide whether to delay, drop, or reject work.
Reservation or hold with expiry: protect scarce inventory
Transactional outbox
Change Data Capture (CDC)
Producers are responsible for publishing messages to an exchange. The library provides both single and batched publish operations.

Borrow / Return
A producer borrows a channel, uses it for one or more publish operations, and returns it to the pool.
The pool tracks which channels are in use to prevent concurrent access (an AMQP channel is not thread-safe).

results.header: How CDC Tracks Its Position (LSN / Offsets)
results.text:
4. Handling "At-Least-Once" Delivery & Duplicate Data
Because committing the offset happens after sending the event to Kafka, a crash can occasionally lead to a scenario where LSN 580 was sent to Kafka, but the CDC engine crashed before updating its offset state to 580. When it recovers, it reads from LSN 410 again and re-sends LSN 580 to Kafka. This means CDC systems guarantee "At-Least-Once" event delivery, so downstream consumers (like your cache, search index, or microservices) must handle occasional duplicate events gracefully.

turn.rewritten_query:
What happens if it crashes before sending the acknowledgement?
Previous user question: I want to avoid losing work when a RabbitMQ consumer crashes. Should I use automatic or manual acknowledgements?
Previous answer (reference only): Manual acknowledgement (autoAck: false) .

results.text:
Auto acknowledgement (autoAck: true) The broker considers a message delivered as soon as it sends it over the socket.
Fastest, no risk of forgetting to ack.
Messages can be lost if the consumer crashes before processing.

Manual acknowledgement (autoAck: false) The application must explicitly call channel.ack(deliveryTag) after successful processing.
nack (or reject) can be used with requeue=true to return the message to the queue, or requeue=false to dead-letter it (if DLX is configured).
Gives full control over at-least-once delivery semantics.

results.header: How CDC Tracks Its Position (LSN / Offsets)
results.text:
3. What Happens During a Crash?
Imagine the CDC engine crashes while processing LSN 580:
flowchart LR
  A["LSN 100"] --> B["LSN 250"] --> C["LSN 410 - Last committed offset"] --> D["LSN 580 - Process crashes here 💥"] --> E["LSN 720"]
  C -.->|"Resume from LSN 411 on restart"| D

The Recovery Sequence:
Restart: The CDC process restarts (e.g., Kubernetes boots up a new container).
Fetch Offset: The CDC engine connects to Kafka and asks: "Where did I leave off?" Kafka responds: "Your last saved position was LSN 410."
Re-attach to DB: The CDC engine opens a connection to the PostgreSQL database and requests: "Start streaming the WAL from LSN 410 onwards."
Resume: The database skips LSNs 100-410 and begins streaming immediately from LSN 411.

Without Publisher Confirms
basic.publish returns as soon as the TCP stack accepts the data. The broker may later fail to route the message (e.g., exchange does not exist, queue is full, disk write error after memory alarm).
Loss scenarios include:
Target exchange missing → message silently dropped unless mandatory flag is used.
Queue overflow with x-max-length → message dead-lettered or dropped.
Broker crash before fsync → durable messages may be lost.

With confirms, the producer knows exactly when the broker has accepted responsibility for the message.

Don't Base64 encode large files. Use multipart/form-data for uploads and binary streaming with correct Content-Type headers for downloads.
Apply dual-layer limiting. Use Infrastructure-level limiting (e.g., Nginx, API Gateway) to stop DDoS, and Application-level limiting (e.g., Redis Token Bucket) for business rules per user/tenant.
Use pagination (cursor-based preferred over offset-based for large datasets[^2]), filtering, and sorting on all collection endpoints.
All internal APIs must accept and use standard Tracing Headers (e.g., W3C traceparent or B3 headers[^6]) to ensure we can debug a request across microservices.
For batch/bulk operations, clarify whether it's an Atomic Transaction or allows 'Partial Success'. If partial success is allowed, the response structure must explicitly map individual IDs to their success/error status.
For long running operations do not block the HTTP request. Return 202 Accepted with a Location header pointing to a status polling endpoint, or use Webhooks.

cases.query: Why does the token comparison matter?

turn.query: Why does the token comparison matter?

results.text:
Just because two companies had an acquisition relation doesn't mean three sentences describe the same acquisition (e.g., Company A might have bought a subsidiary of Company B in 2010, and another in 2022).
The system checks Contextual Slots:
Temporal Overlap: Do timestamps (2016) match or fit within the same timeframe window?
Numerical Alignment: Do values ($2.6B, all-stock) reinforce or at least not contradict each other?
Directional Consistency: Was Subject → Object active, or Object ← Subject passive?

If the slots align without logical contradictions, the confidence that these three sources refer to the same event approaches 100%.

The identity pipeline uses external OAuth2 tokens for clients and internal Passports for microservices.
External authentication (OAuth2): On login, the Identity Service issues a short-lived access token and a refresh token. Mobile clients send the access token in the Authorization header.
Identity Passport pattern: The Edge Gateway exchanges the public token for a signed Passport containing validated user metadata. Services can verify it locally instead of calling the Identity Service.
{
  "user_id": "usr_9921_sf",
  "user_type": "DRIVER",
  "device_id": "dev_iphone_8832",
  "authenticated_at": 1770562800,
  "scopes": ["trips:read", "location:write"]
}

The Passport is HMAC-signed with a key shared across the internal mesh. Services verify the signature locally.
Service-to-service security (SPIFFE/SPIRE and mTLS): Each workload receives a cryptographic identity. SPIRE issues short-lived X.509 certificates, and sidecar proxies enforce which services may communicate.

A Redis lock is a temporary marker that lets one worker claim a job. SET lock:resource <token> NX PX <milliseconds> creates the marker only if it does not exist (NX) and sets an expiry time (PX). Give each attempt a different token so Redis can tell which worker owns the marker.

Not all extracted statements carry equal factual or causal weight. An unverified tweet and an official SEC filing should not create edges with identical authority.
Edge Attributes: Every edge retains metadata properties:
confidence_score: Probability assigned by the extraction model (0.0–1.0).
source_count: How many independent sources verified this exact relationship.
timestamp / decay_rate: How recent the edge is.

Threshold Filtering: Graph visualization and pathfinding algorithms dynamically filter out edges below a minimum confidence or source count threshold, automatically collapsing noise.

When the worker finishes, it should delete the marker only if the token still matches. Otherwise, a worker whose lock has expired could accidentally delete a newer worker's lock. The lock can also expire while work is still running, allowing another worker to start the same job. For important changes, make the operation safe to repeat or enforce uniqueness in the database that stores the result. A lock alone cannot prevent duplicate work after it expires

cases.query: What about separate processes: can they share the same virtual address?

turn.query: What about separate processes: can they share the same virtual address?

results.text:
Each process uses a virtual address space that the OS and hardware map to physical memory. For example, different processes can use the same virtual address without referring to the same physical address.
Process A                         Process B
Virtual address space             Virtual address space
+---------------+                 +---------------+
| 0x0000        |---+         +---| 0x0000        |
| ...           |   |         |   | ...           |
| 0x1000        |---+         +---| 0x1000        |

thread’s stack memory if it has a valid pointer to that memory.
Separate processes have separate address spaces, so their heaps, global data, and stacks are isolated from one another unless they explicitly use an inter-process sharing mechanism.

Even when Redis and the app run on one machine or in one container host, they remain separate processes communicating over a socket. A separate Redis service is useful when app instances need shared state or when Redis needs independent memory, scaling, and operations.

Each thread uses its stack for local variables, function calls, and return addresses. Threads in the same process share the code, heap, and global or static data. Shared heap and global data may require synchronization when multiple threads access it concurrently.
Note: A thread can access another thread’s stack memory if it has a valid pointer to that memory.
